summary.central_question: Why have China's retaliatory tariffs crushed U.S. commodity exports while barely denting U.S. manufacturing exports to China?
summary.main_thesis: China's retaliation has so far bitten mainly through commodities; its manufacturing tariffs have had modest effect, and bilateral trade declines should not be equated with overall trade or output losses.

content.text: Why have China's retaliatory tariffs crushed U.S. commodity exports while barely denting U.S. manufacturing exports to China?
content.reason: A puzzle arises when similar policy instruments produce very different effects across sectors.

passages.source_excerpt: One set of tariffs (on commodities) has had a very large impact: exports are down over 60 percent, and the fall isn't over

content.text: The author expected a bigger fall in U.S. manufacturing exports to China and admits the modest decline surprised him.
content.reason: An analyst should flag when outcomes contradict his own prior expectation.

passages.source_excerpt: Somewhat to my surprise to be honest.

content.text: Raising tariffs on a substantial share of goods should, after enough time, show up as a visible decline in those exports.
content.reason: Tariffs raise prices to buyers and so should reduce the volume of tariffed imports over time.

passages.source_excerpt: it did put tariffs on a decent chunk of U.S. manufacturing exports (see Bown's figure 3). So there should be some impact

content.text: Chad Bown's work shows China tariffed 55% of U.S. exports, raised its effective tariff from 8% to 18%, left aircraft out, and refrained from re-raising auto tariffs.
content.reason: Trade-policy trackers by specialist researchers provide the coverage of tariff actions.

passages.source_excerpt: China, per Chad Bown of the Peterson Institute, has only put tariffs on 55 percent of U.S. goods exports

content.text: Soybeans are ~10% of U.S. exports to China; commodity exports fell over 60% while manufacturing exports show no visible break, with only a somewhat larger U.S. than European drop last fall.
content.reason: Trailing sums of sectoral export data reveal whether a policy shock leaves a visible break.

passages.source_excerpt: Soybeans traditionally have accounted for about 10 percent of total U.S. (goods) exports to China

content.text: Comparing U.S. manufacturing exports with euro area exports to China shows some tariff impact, though partly attributable to dollar strength.
content.reason: A comparable peer's exports to the same market serve as a control for demand shocks.

passages.source_excerpt: There was a bigger drop off in American exports to China than in European exports to China last fall

content.text: Part of the relative U.S. underperformance could reflect the dollar's appreciation rather than tariffs.
content.reason: Exchange rate moves affect relative export performance with lags of years.

passages.source_excerpt: though not one so big that it could not be, in part, a function of the dollar's strength relative to the euro

content.text: China has held back from fully squeezing some sectors, such as autos, to keep targets in reserve for future escalation.
content.reason: In repeated bargaining a party preserves leverage by not using all its retaliation at once.

passages.source_excerpt: China has exercised a bit of restraint, and held back on really restricting trade in some sectors to make sure it has targets to retaliate against

reasons: links: `P3` motivates `M1` joins L1→L3, which no hand-drawn motivates link does

content.text: China lacks good targets because many U.S. manufactured imports have no domestic substitute or feed China's own exports, so tariffs would hurt China.
content.reason: Tariffs on non-substitutable or input goods mainly tax the importing country's own firms.

passages.source_excerpt: China lacks good targets, as the bulk of its manufactured imports from the United States are in sectors where there isn't (for now) a domestic Chinese alternative

content.text: Industrial policy and high pre-existing tariffs already pushed U.S. exports out of sectors like construction equipment, removing them as targets.
content.reason: A market already closed by import substitution offers little further room for retaliation.

passages.source_excerpt: China's relatively high initial tariffs and its efforts to encourage "indigenous" production have already limited U.S. exports in some important sectors.

reasons: links: `M3` rebuts `X` joins L3→L6, which no hand-drawn rebuts link does

content.text: U.S. construction equipment exports to China fell from about $2 billion in 2012 to $0.6-0.8 billion pre-trade war, and the U.S. runs deficits with China in construction and telecom equipment.
content.reason: Sector-level export histories show whether a supposed target still exists.

passages.source_excerpt: Exports of construction and agricultural equipment/ NAICS 3331 to China peaked at around $2 billion in 2012. They were running at between 0.6 and 0.8 billion a year before the trade war.

content.text: Commentators who assume China can easily retaliate against U.S. construction and switching equipment rely on an outdated picture of U.S. exports.
content.reason: Claims about trade leverage must be checked against current trade composition.

passages.source_excerpt: I am often a little frustrated by otherwise well informed commentators who have an out-of-date concept of what the U.S. exports to China.

reasons: links: `M3` rebuts `X` joins L3→L6, which no hand-drawn rebuts link does

content.text: Soy exports to China went to zero, consistent with high trade elasticities found in many studies.
content.reason: For homogeneous goods with many suppliers, demand is highly price-elastic to tariffs.

passages.source_excerpt: With an elasticity of 4, a 25 percent tariff would be expected to zero out trade.

content.text: The soy collapse may instead reflect state importers being directed not to buy U.S. beans, which cost them little given the discount.
content.reason: Where state-owned firms dominate imports, political directives can substitute for price effects.

passages.source_excerpt: But it is also consistent with a world where China's state importing companies were told not to buy American.

content.text: Soy losses to China were not offset elsewhere, so the tariff cut total U.S. soy exports and hurt farmers, with 2019 exports likely modest regardless of a deal.
content.reason: When the targeted buyer is dominant, exporters cannot fully redirect sales to others.

passages.source_excerpt: The reduction in China's purchases of soybeans clearly hurt American farmers who weren't able to make up for the fall in Chinese demand

content.text: Oil exports to China fell to near zero but total U.S. oil exports and pipeline investment were unaffected because oil is easily redirected.
content.reason: In a true global commodity market, a bilateral tariff diverts trade rather than reducing it.

passages.source_excerpt: The tariffs diverted bilateral trade in oil away from China without impacting overall trade.

content.text: Auto exports to China fell then rebounded, and BMW and Mercedes appear to have offset lost China sales with rising U.S. SUV demand, leaving production plans largely intact.
content.reason: Producers can absorb a lost export market by reallocating output to growing domestic demand.

passages.source_excerpt: it is possible that Mercedes and BMW were effectively able to offset their reduced exports to China by producing more for the U.S. market.

content.text: U.S. auto exports to China would likely fall anyway as German firms localize production in China, making the tariff effect hard to isolate.
content.reason: Structural trends can mimic policy effects, complicating causal attribution.

passages.source_excerpt: The counterfactual here is hard.

content.text: Firms and exporters that lose one market can find alternative buyers or uses, so bilateral losses need not translate into aggregate losses.
content.reason: Markets reallocate goods across buyers when one buyer withdraws, if substitutes exist.

content.text: China's retaliation has so far bitten mainly through commodities; its manufacturing tariffs have had modest effect, and bilateral trade declines should not be equated with overall trade or output losses.
content.reason: The aggregate impact of a tariff depends on how easily the affected sector can redirect its sales.

passages.source_excerpt: Don't equate changes in bilateral trade with changes in overall trade, or changes in total output. A lot depends on the sector.

content.text: The modest manufacturing elasticity may partly reflect untariffed goods in the aggregate, since he did not disaggregate tariffed from untariffed products.
content.reason: Aggregates mixing treated and untreated goods understate the effect on the treated.

passages.source_excerpt: but I haven't tried to disaggregate manufactures into those actually tariffed by China and those that have escaped so far

content.text: The overall impact of China's retaliation on the U.S. economy remains an open question.
content.reason: Early data on trade shocks warrant provisional conclusions.

passages.source_excerpt: the debate on the overall impact of China's retaliation on the U.S. economy is sure to continue

content.text: Commentators should consult end-use trade data before assessing retaliation targets.
content.reason: Detailed product-level data should ground claims about trade leverage.

passages.source_excerpt: Do look at the end use data, which is easy to use
